<h1>Phase Portraits & Stability Analysis: Invariant Manifolds & Limit Cycles</h1>
<p class="hero-lead">
Locate equilibrium points and classify their local topology in the <span class="highlight-blue">trace-determinant plane $(\tau, \Delta)$</span> 
of the Jacobian matrix. Map stable and unstable <span class="highlight-orange">invariant manifolds</span>, and explore 
isolated self-excited periodic orbits—<span class="highlight-teal">limit cycles</span>—in the Van der Pol oscillator.
</p>

<!-- Section 2: Theory -->
<section class="lesson-section" id="sec-theory">
<div class="section-header">
<div class="section-tag">01 · Local Linearization</div>
<h2>6.1 The Jacobian Matrix & Characteristic Roots</h2>
<p>For an autonomous planar dynamical system $\dot{x}_1 = f_1(x_1, x_2)$, $\dot{x}_2 = f_2(x_1, x_2)$ with equilibrium fixed point $\mathbf{x}^*$:</p>
</div>

<div class="card">
<div class="eq-box">
$$\mathbf{J} = \left.\begin{bmatrix} \frac{\partial f_1}{\partial x_1} & \frac{\partial f_1}{\partial x_2} \\ \frac{\partial f_2}{\partial x_1} & \frac{\partial f_2}{\partial x_2} \end{bmatrix}\right|_{\mathbf{x}^*}, \quad \lambda^2 - \tau \lambda + \Delta = 0$$
</div>

<p>
Where the trace $\tau$ and determinant $\Delta$ evaluate directly to:
</p>

<div class="eq-box">
$$\tau = \operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{J}) = \lambda_1 + \lambda_2, \quad \Delta = \det(\mathbf{J}) = \lambda_1 \lambda_2 \quad \implies \quad \lambda_{1,2} = \frac{\tau \pm \sqrt{\tau^2 - 4\Delta}}{2}$$
</div>
</div>
</section>

<!-- Section 3: Stability Plane -->
<section class="lesson-section" id="sec-stability">
<div class="section-header">
<div class="section-tag">02 · Geometric Topology</div>
<h2>6.2 The Trace-Determinant Diagram</h2>
<p>The parabola $\tau^2 - 4\Delta = 0$ partitions the $(\tau, \Delta)$ parameter plane into distinct topological regimes.</p>
</div>

<div class="card">
<div class="callout">
<strong>• Saddle Points ($\Delta < 0$):</strong> One positive and one negative real eigenvalue; always unstable with distinct incoming (stable) and outgoing (unstable) invariant manifolds.<br>
<strong>• Stable Nodes ($\Delta > 0, \tau < 0, \tau^2 > 4\Delta$):</strong> Real negative eigenvalues; pure exponential decay without oscillation.<br>
<strong>• Stable Spirals ($\Delta > 0, \tau < 0, \tau^2 < 4\Delta$):</strong> Complex conjugate eigenvalues with negative real part; decaying oscillatory trajectories.<br>
<strong>• Center Points ($\tau = 0, \Delta > 0$):</strong> Purely imaginary eigenvalues; neutrally stable continuous concentric orbits.<br>
<strong>• Hopf Bifurcation ($\tau$ crosses zero with $\Delta > 0$):</strong> Transition from stable focus to unstable focus with the spontaneous birth of an isolated limit cycle.
</div>
</div>
</section>

<!-- Section 4: Misconceptions -->
<section class="lesson-section" id="sec-misconceptions">
<div class="callout-important">
<div class="callout-title">
<svg width="20" height="20" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"><path d="M10.29 3.86L1.82 18a2 2 0 0 0 1.71 3h16.94a2 2 0 0 0 1.71-3L13.71 3.86a2 2 0 0 0-3.42 0z"/><line x1="12" y1="9" x2="12" y2="13"/><line x1="12" y1="17" x2="12.01" y2="17"/></svg>
Common Misconception · Are Limit Cycles Just Linear Harmonic Oscillations?
</div>
<p style="margin: 0 0 8px 0;">
Students often view limit cycles as simple periodic orbits identical to undamped mass-spring harmonic oscillations.
</p>
<p style="margin: 0;">
<strong>They are fundamentally different.</strong> In a linear conservative system, there are infinite continuous families of periodic orbits—perturbing the amplitude creates a new orbit. In contrast, a <em>limit cycle</em> is an <strong>isolated periodic trajectory</strong> in a dissipative, self-excited nonlinear system. Perturbed trajectories inside or outside the limit cycle are drawn into it asymptotically!
</p>
</div>
</section>

<!-- Section 5: Quiz -->
<section class="lesson-section" id="sec-quiz">
<div class="section-header">
<div class="section-tag">03 · Diagnostic Checkpoint</div>
<h2>6.3 Check Your Understanding</h2>
<p>Test your understanding of the trace-determinant stability plane.</p>
</div>

<div class="quiz-box">
<div class="quiz-question">
<strong>Question:</strong> An autonomous system linearized about fixed point $(0,0)$ yields Jacobian matrix $\mathbf{J} = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 3 \\ -4 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$. What is the topological classification of this equilibrium point?
</div>
<div class="quiz-options">
<div class="quiz-opt" data-correct="false" data-explanation="Delta = (-2)(-1) - (3)(-4) = 2 + 12 = 14 > 0. Since Delta > 0, it CANNOT be a saddle point!">
A. Saddle point.
</div>
<div class="quiz-opt" data-correct="true" data-explanation="Trace tau = -2 + (-1) = -3 < 0. Determinant Delta = (-2)(-1) - (3)(-4) = 2 + 12 = 14 > 0. Check discriminant: tau^2 - 4*Delta = (-3)^2 - 4(14) = 9 - 56 = -47 < 0. Since Delta > 0, tau < 0, and discriminant < 0, the eigenvalues are complex conjugate with negative real part: a Stable Focus (Spiral)!">
B. Stable Spiral (Focus).
</div>
<div class="quiz-opt" data-correct="false" data-explanation="Discriminant tau^2 - 4*Delta = 9 - 56 = -47 < 0, which yields complex eigenvalues with oscillations, not real non-oscillatory node decay.">
C. Stable Node.
</div>
</div>
<div class="quiz-feedback"></div>
</div>

<!-- Section 6: Code -->
<section class="lesson-section" id="sec-code">
<div class="section-header">
<div class="section-tag">04 · Computational Implementation</div>
<h2>6.4 Van der Pol Limit Cycle Integration</h2>
<p>Simulate phase portraits and asymptotic convergence to the Van der Pol limit cycle in Python.</p>
</div>

<div class="code-box">
<div class="code-header">
<div class="code-tabs">
<button class="code-tab-btn active">Python (SciPy solve_ivp)</button>
</div>
<button class="btn-copy">Copy Code</button>
</div>
<pre class="code-block"><code>import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp

# Van der Pol Oscillator: x'' - mu*(1 - x^2)*x' + x = 0
mu = 1.0

def vdp_system(t, state):
    x, y = state
    return [y, mu * (1.0 - x**2) * y - x]

# Integrate from interior and exterior initial states
sol_inner = solve_ivp(vdp_system, [0, 30], [0.1, 0.1], max_step=0.02)
sol_outer = solve_ivp(vdp_system, [0, 30], [3.0, 3.0], max_step=0.02)

print("Both trajectories converge asymptotically onto the unique isolated limit cycle!")</code></pre>
</div>
